blocks.label: Hydrocarbons
blocks.text: Compounds of carbon and hydrogen only are called hydrocarbons.

blocks.head: Classification of Hydrocarbons
blocks.body: Hydrocarbons are broadly divided into two classes:
items: Aliphatic — not aromatic; may be open chain or cyclic, saturated or unsaturated
Aromatic — special cyclic class based on benzene ring; have high C:H ratio

blocks.label: Aliphatic Hydrocarbons
blocks.text: The compounds that are not aromatic are called aliphatic hydrocarbons. Aliphatic compounds may be open chain and cyclic, also they may be saturated or unsaturated.

blocks.label: Aromatic Hydrocarbons
blocks.text: Aromatic hydrocarbons is a special class of cyclic hydrocarbons that have high carbon to hydrogen ratio and are based on benzene (C₆H₆) or resembling compounds.

blocks.head: Did You Know?
blocks.body: The term 'aromatic' comes from the Greek word 'aroma' meaning fragrance. It describes compounds with characteristic odour.

blocks.label: Alkanes
blocks.text: Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons with the general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂.

blocks.head: General Formulas
blocks.body: Key general formulas to memorize:
blocks.eq:
Alkane      → CₙH₂ₙ₊₂
Cycloalkane → CₙH₂ₙ
Alkene      → CₙH₂ₙ
Alkyne      → CₙH₂ₙ₋₂

blocks.head: Did You Know?
blocks.body: Butane is a fuel used in lighters. Isobutane is used as a propellant in shaving gel.

blocks.label: Alkyl Group
blocks.text: Derivations of alkanes with less hydrogen than in alkanes. Formed by removing one H atom from an alkane. Represented by 'R'. General formula: CₙH₂ₙ₊₁.

blocks.head: Types of Alkyl Groups
blocks.body: Alkyl groups are classified by which carbon the H is removed from:
items: Primary alkyl: H removed from terminal (end) carbon — e.g. n-propyl (CH₃CH₂CH₂–)
Secondary alkyl: H removed from carbon with 2 adjacent carbons — e.g. sec-butyl
Tertiary alkyl: H removed from carbon with 3 adjacent carbons — prefixed 'neo'

blocks.head: Prefix
blocks.body: Comes before the name of the compound. May be alphabets or numbers.
items: Alphabets: n (normal/straight), iso (branched), neo (one C with 4 adjacent C), di, tri, tetra
Numbers: tell position of side group or functional group

blocks.head: Suffix
blocks.body: Initial + suffix → compound name. Suffix tells the nature of the compound.
blocks.eq:
–ane   → alkane
–ene   → alkene
–yne   → alkyne
–ol    → alcohol (R–OH)
–al    → aldehyde (R–CHO)
–one   → ketone (R–COR)
–oic acid → carboxyl (R–COOH)

blocks.head: Nature of Chain
blocks.body: Chain type is indicated by prefix:
items: n-chain → straight chain
iso/neo-chain → branched chain
For iso: carbons are equally distributed around central atom
For neo: one carbon has 4 adjacent carbons

items.title: Selection of Parent Chain
items.body: — Contains maximum number of carbon atoms AND maximum number of substituents. May not always be straight.

items.title: Numbering of Chain
items.body: — With one substituent: start from the end nearest the substituent so it gets lowest position number.

items.title: Two or more substituents
items.body: — With different substituents: start from side where one substituent gets lowest position (no competition). If competing, prefer larger substituent at lower position.

items.title: Two similar substituents
items.body: — If competing → prefer either side. If not competing → prefer side where one of them gets lower position.

items.title: Naming Format
items.body: — Use comma between two numbers. Use hyphen (-) between name and number. Use di, tri, tetra as prefix for identical substituents.

blocks.head: Naming Sequence
blocks.body: Final name format:
blocks.eq: position of substituent + name of substituent + parent chain name as alkane

blocks.head: What is a Substituent?
blocks.body: Not part of the long (parent) chain. Known as side group. Always has fewer carbons than parent chain. In IUPAC naming, substituent is NOT counted in the long chain.
items: iso-butyl: CH₃–CH(CH₃)–CH₂–
n-butyl: CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂–
sec-butyl: CH₃CH₂CH(CH₃)–
tert-butyl (neo): (CH₃)₃C–

blocks.head: Structure of Cycloalkanes
blocks.body: Cycloalkanes are cyclic — carbon atoms arranged in ring form. They are saturated (only single bonds). They have a changed ring angle compared to open-chain alkanes.
items: Cyclopropane: C₃H₆ — triangle shape
Cyclobutane: C₄H₈
Cyclopentane: C₅H₁₀
Cyclohexane: C₆H₁₂

blocks.caption: Structural shapes of cyclopropane, cyclobutane, cyclopentane, cyclohexane
blocks.alt: Ring structures of cycloalkanes from 3 to 6 carbons

blocks.head: Naming Cycloalkanes
blocks.body: Naming format:
blocks.eq: position of side group + name of side group + cyclo + name of alkane

items.title: Start numbering at carbon where substituent is present
For more than one substituent
items.body: — start at carbon where maximum substituent gets lowest position

items.title: If two methyl groups in side
items.body: — consider them as two separate groups

items.q: Write down the structural formulas for 2-Methylbutane and 2,2-Dimethylpropane.
items.ans:
2-Methylbutane:

CH₃–CH(CH₃)–CH₂–CH₃

2,2-Dimethylpropane:

CH₃ | CH₃–C–CH₃ | CH₃

items.q: Write down displayed formula of 2,3,3-Trimethylhexane and Methylcyclohexane.
items.ans:
2,3,3-Trimethylhexane: 6-carbon parent chain with CH₃ at C2, and two CH₃ at C3.

Methylcyclohexane: Cyclohexane ring with one CH₃ group attached.

items.q: Give two differences between molecules of cyclopentane and pentane.
items.ans:
• Cyclopentane (C₅H₁₀) is cyclic; pentane (C₅H₁₂) is open chain.
  • Cyclopentane has no isomers (only one structure); pentane has three isomers.

items.q: Eicosane is a straight chain alkane whose molecules contain 20 carbon atoms. What is the molecular formula of eicosane?
items.ans:
Using CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ where n = 20:

C₂₀H₄₂

blocks.head: Structure of Alkanes
blocks.body: Each carbon in alkanes is sp³ hybridized. Alkane molecules have tetrahedral shape around each carbon.
items: Atomic number of Carbon = 6
Ground state: 1s² 2s² 2px¹ 2py¹ 2pz⁰
Excited state: 1s² 2s¹ 2px¹ 2py¹ 2pz¹
Hybridized state: 1s² 2sp³ 2sp³ 2sp³ 2sp³

blocks.caption: sp³ orbital diagram of carbon showing 2s, 2px, 2py, 2pz combining into four sp³ hybrid orbitals
blocks.alt: Four sp³ hybrid orbitals arranged tetrahedrally

blocks.head: Orientation (Tetrahedral Shape)
blocks.body: Four sp³ orbitals repel equally to give:
items: Bond angle: 109.5°
Bond length (C–C): 1.54 Å
Tetrahedral geometry

blocks.caption: Tetrahedral shape of methane and ethane with bond angle 109.5° and bond length 1.54 Å
blocks.alt: Ball-and-stick models of methane and ethane

blocks.head: Bonding in Alkanes
blocks.body: All bonds in alkanes are sigma (σ) bonds — no π bonds.
items: C–C σ-bond: formed by sp³–sp³ head-on overlapping
C–H σ-bond: formed by s–sp³ overlapping
No unhybridized orbitals → no π bonds

blocks.head: Shapes of Cycloalkanes
blocks.body: Cycloalkanes have ring structure with all sp³ carbons. Ring strain changes the ideal bond angles.
items: Cyclopropane (C₃H₆): triangular — highest ring strain
Cyclopentane (C₅H₁₀): envelope shape
Cyclohexane (C₆H₁₂): chair/boat — most stable, least strain

blocks.head: State at Room Temperature
blocks.body: Physical state depends on carbon number:
items: C₁ to C₄ → gases
C₅ to C₁₇ → liquids
C₁₈ onwards → waxy solids

blocks.head: Polarity
blocks.body: Alkanes are non-polar or very weakly polar.
items: EN of C = 2.5, EN of H = 2.1
ΔEN = 2.5 – 2.1 = 0.4 (non-polar range: 0–0.4)
So C–H bond is non-polar; C–C bond is also non-polar

blocks.head: Solubility
blocks.body: Insoluble in polar solvents like water. Soluble in non-polar solvents like benzene, ether, hexane.

blocks.head: Physical Constants
blocks.body: Boiling point, melting point, density all increase with carbon number. Solubility decreases with increase in carbon number.
items: Branched chain alkanes have lower BP than straight chain isomers
Example: n-butane BP = –0.5°C > iso-butane BP = –11.7°C
Reason: straight chain has more surface area → stronger London dispersion forces

items.q: Why do branched alkanes have lower boiling points than straight-chain alkanes?
items.ans:
Branched alkanes have weaker intermolecular (London dispersion) forces. Branches reduce surface area, so less contact between molecules, resulting in weaker forces and lower boiling points.

Straight chain provides more surface area → stronger London dispersion forces → higher BP.

Example: n-butane (BP –0.5°C) > iso-butane (BP –11.7°C)

items.q: Explain why alkanes have a tetrahedral shape.
items.ans: Each carbon in alkanes forms 4 covalent bonds. The carbons are sp³ hybridized. Four bonding pairs of electrons equally repel each other and arrange themselves at 109.5° — tetrahedral geometry.

items.q: Draw the shapes of cyclopropane and cyclopentane.
items.ans: See diagram block — cyclopropane is triangular (C₃H₆) and cyclopentane is envelope-shaped (C₅H₁₀).

sections.title: Reaction Mechanism and Modes of Bond Breaking

blocks.label: Reaction Mechanism
blocks.text: Reaction mechanism is the series of steps that take place in the course of the overall reaction.

blocks.label: Fission
blocks.text: Breakage of bonds is called fission. It is a dissociation process. Two forms: Homolytic and Heterolytic.

blocks.label: Homolytic Fission
blocks.text: Breakage of bond in which electrons of bond pair are distributed evenly between two separating atoms.

blocks.head: Homolytic Fission — Key Points
blocks.body: Features of homolytic fission:
items: Forms two free radicals
Usually occurs in presence of light in atomic reactions
Represented by half-headed (fish-hook) arrows: (↼ ⇁)
Cl–Cl → Cl• + Cl•

blocks.label: Free Radical
blocks.text: Free Radical is a species that contains an unpaired electron and is very reactive.

blocks.label: Heterolytic Fission
blocks.text: Breakage of bond in which electrons of bond pair are unevenly distributed between two separating atoms.

blocks.head: Heterolytic Fission — Key Points
blocks.body: Features of heterolytic fission:
items: Forms two oppositely charged ions
Usually occurs in ionic reactions
Represented by complete single-headed (full curly) arrow
HO–H → OH⁻ + H⁺

blocks.caption: Comparison of homolytic and heterolytic fission with arrow notation
blocks.alt: Two diagrams: homolytic with half arrows forming radicals, heterolytic with full arrow forming ions

sections.title: Unreactive Nature of Alkanes Towards Polar Reagents

blocks.head: Why Alkanes Are Called Paraffins
blocks.body: Alkanes are called paraffins (Latin: parum = little, affins = affinity). They are inert towards acids, alkalis, oxidizing and reducing agents under ordinary conditions.
items: Alkanes are least reactive
Called paraffins (para → less reactivity, affin → reactivity)

blocks.head: Reactivity Depends On
blocks.body: Two factors determine reactivity of alkanes:
items: i) Polarity — if polarity is high, reactivity is also high
ii) Inertness of bond

blocks.head: i) Polarity
blocks.body: Polarity increases with ΔEN (electronegativity difference):
items: ΔEN 0–0.4 → non-polar
ΔEN 0.4–1.7 → polar
EN of C = 2.5, EN of H = 2.1
ΔEN = 2.5 – 2.1 = 0.4 → C–H bond is non-polar
C–C bond is also non-polar (same atoms)
blocks.eq: So, C–H and C–C bonds are non-polar → alkanes are least reactive

blocks.head: ii) Inertness of Bond
blocks.body: C–C and C–H bonds are σ-bonds.
items: Electrons of sigma bonds are tightly held between two nuclei
So electrons are not easily available
It means bonds show inertness

blocks.head: Conclusion
blocks.body: Due to non-polarity and bond inertness, alkanes are least reactive — called paraffins.

blocks.head: Types of Reactions Alkanes Give
blocks.body: Alkanes undergo:
items: i. Substitution reactions
ii. Catalytic reactions → oxidation / cracking

sections.title: Reactions of Alkanes — Free Radical Substitution

blocks.label: Substitution Reaction
blocks.text: Reaction in which atoms or groups of atoms are replaced by another atom or group.

blocks.label: Halogenation of Alkanes
blocks.text: Substitution reaction of alkanes that replaces hydrogen with halogen is called halogenation.

blocks.head: Effect of Electronegativty (EN) on Reactivity
blocks.body: The rate of halogenation depends on EN and size of halogen:
items: EN order: F₂ > Cl₂ > Br₂ > I₂
Size order: F₂ < Cl₂ < Br₂ < I₂ (size inversely affects rate)
Reactivity order: F₂ > Cl₂ > Br₂ > I₂

blocks.head: Effect of Each Halogen
blocks.body: Each halogen behaves differently:
items: Fluorination: very vigorous reaction → causes explosion → never forms CH₃F or CH₂CHF → poly-fluorinated products formed (CHF₃, CF₄) → NOT preferred
Cl₂ and Br₂: react moderately → preferred → follow free radical mechanism
Iodination: very slow → requires HNO₃ and HIO₄

blocks.head: Effect of Light on Halogenation Rate
blocks.body: Light intensity affects reaction rate:
items: Bright light → vigorous reaction → CH₄ + 2Cl₂ →(hν)→ C + 4HCl (carbon black formed)
Diffused light → mixture of products by free radical propagation

blocks.head: Factors Affecting Rate of Reaction
blocks.body: Rate of reaction depends on:
items: EN of halogen
Size (inversely)
Concentration
Intensity of light

blocks.head: Mechanism Overview
blocks.body: Halogenation follows free radical mechanism with 3 steps:
items: 1. Initiation
2. Propagation
3. Termination

blocks.head: Step 1: Initiation
blocks.body: Starts by homolytic breakage of Cl–Cl bond. Diffused light produces two Cl• free radicals. Cl• are highly unstable.

blocks.head: Step 2: Propagation
blocks.body: Cl• attacks at C–H bond. Carbon free radical forms. C• attacks Cl₂ molecule.
blocks.eq:
H–C–H + Cl• → H–C• + HCl
H–C• + Cl–Cl → H–C–Cl + Cl•

blocks.caption: Propagation steps of free radical chlorination of methane showing formation of CH₃Cl, CH₂Cl₂, CHCl₃, CCl₄
blocks.alt: Chain of propagation steps from methane to tetrachloromethane

blocks.head: Step 3: Termination
blocks.body: Reaction can be terminated by:
items: i. By removing alkanes or Cl₂
ii. By removing light
iii. By combining two free radicals together:
blocks.eq:
Cl• + Cl• → Cl₂
CH₃• + Cl• → CH₃Cl
CH₃• + CH₃• → C₂H₆ (minor product)

blocks.head: Interesting Information
blocks.body: Haloalkanes are anaesthetic in nature. The anaesthetic power increases with number of halogen atoms. They are strictly monitored as organic solvents due to toxic nature.

blocks.head: Free Radical Substitution of Ethane
blocks.body: Free radical substitution of ethane results in formation of hexachloroethane (C₂Cl₆).

items.q: Explain why alkanes have high stability?
items.ans:
Alkanes are stable because:
1. C–H and C–C bonds are non-polar (ΔEN = 0.4) — polar reagents cannot attack.
2. Sigma bonds hold electrons tightly between nuclei → not easily available → bond inertness.

items.q: What are major types of reactions that alkanes undergo?
items.ans:
• Substitution (halogenation)
  • Catalytic reactions: oxidation and cracking

items.q: How does the termination step occur in halogenation of alkanes?
items.ans:
Termination occurs when two free radicals combine to form a stable product:

Cl• + Cl• → Cl₂ CH₃• + Cl• → CH₃Cl CH₃• + CH₃• → C₂H₆

Reaction can also be terminated by removing alkanes, Cl₂, or light source.

items.q: State the conditions under which a mixture of halogenoalkanes is obtained from halogenation of alkanes.
items.ans: Conditions: diffused light and inert solvent. Under these conditions, free radical propagation continues stepwise replacing one H at a time, giving a mixture: CH₃Cl → CH₂Cl₂ → CHCl₃ → CCl₄.

items.q: Predict the products of free radical chlorination of ethane.
items.ans: Products: C₂H₅Cl → C₂H₄Cl₂ → C₂H₃Cl₃ → C₂H₂Cl₄ → C₂HCl₅ → C₂Cl₆ (hexachloroethane)

blocks.label: Alkenes
blocks.text: Unsaturated hydrocarbons with C=C double bond. General formula CₙH₂ₙ.

blocks.head: Why Alkenes Are Called Olefins
blocks.body: Electrons of π-bond are delocalized. They revolve around nucleus and are easily available. As a result, they act as nucleophile and make alkenes highly reactive. Alkenes are called olefins. They form oily layer with alkyl halides with halogens.

items.title: Selection of Chain
items.body: — Contain both olefinic carbons (C=C). Contain maximum substituents.

items.title: Numbering
items.body: — Start numbering near the double bond regardless of the substituent. If position of double bond is same from either side, prefer lower position of substituent.

items.title: Naming Format
items.body: — position of substituent + name of substituent + position of double bond + name of parent chain as alkene

blocks.label: Elimination Reaction
blocks.text: Reaction in which two atoms or group of atoms are removed from adjacent carbon atoms.

blocks.head: i) Dehydration of Alcohol
blocks.body: Dehydration is the removal of water. A reaction where alkenes react with halogens in the presence of water.
items: Dehydrating agent: conc. H₂SO₄
Temperature: 180°C for H₂SO₄
During reaction: H-atom is removed along with OH-group
Mechanism: formation of alkyl hydrogen sulphonate

blocks.head: ii) Dehydrohalogenation of Alkyl Halide
blocks.body: Monohaloalkanes are called alkyl halides. Removal of hydrogen and halogen from adjacent carbons.
items: Reagents: alcoholic KOH
Removal of H and halogen → creates double bond

blocks.head: Physical Properties
blocks.body: Physical properties of alkenes:
items: C₂ to C₄ → gases; C₅ to C₁₅ → liquids; higher members → solids
Insoluble in water; soluble in alcohol
Characteristic smell; burn with luminous flame
Weakly polar due to sp² hybridization

items.q: Give the reactions of propanol with H₂SO₄, write down all reactions involved.
items.ans:
Step 1: Formation of propyl hydrogen sulphonate:

CH₃CH₂CH₂OH + H₂SO₄ → CH₃CH₂CH₂OSO₃H + H₂O

Step 2: Decomposition on heating:

CH₃CH₂CH₂OSO₃H →(180°C)→ CH₃CH=CH₂ + H₂SO₄

items.q: Give the dehydrohalogenation reaction of bromopropane.
items.ans: CH₃CH₂CH₂Br + KOH(alc.) →(heat)→ CH₃CH=CH₂ + KBr + H₂O

blocks.head: Hybridization of Alkenes
blocks.body: Alkenes are sp² hybridized. Ethene (C₂H₄) is the simplest alkene.
items: Atomic Number of Carbon = 6
Ground state: 1s² 2s² 2px¹ 2py¹
Excited state: 1s² 2s¹ 2px¹ 2py¹ 2pz¹
Hybridized state: 1s² 2sp² 2sp² 2sp² 2pz¹

blocks.caption: sp² orbital diagram of carbon — three sp² hybrid orbitals + one unhybrid pz orbital
blocks.alt: Three sp² orbitals in a plane, unhybrid p orbital perpendicular

blocks.head: Orientation — Trigonal Planar
blocks.body: sp² hybridization gives trigonal planar shape:
items: Orbitals: sp² = 3 (in plane), pz = 1 (perpendicular)
Bond angle: 120°
Trigonal planar shape

blocks.head: Bonding in Ethene
blocks.body: Types of bonds in alkenes:
items: C–C σ-bond: formed by sp²–sp² head-on overlapping
C–H σ-bonds: formed by s–sp² overlapping
C=C π-bond: formed by lateral (sideways) overlap of unhybrid pz orbitals

blocks.caption: Bond formation in ethene showing σ-bonds and π-bond formation
blocks.alt: Ethene with sp² orbitals forming sigma bonds and pz forming pi bond

blocks.head: Shape of Alkene (Ethene)
blocks.body: Ethene (C₂H₄) geometry:
items: Bond angle: 120°
Geometry: Trigonal planar (NOT tetrahedral)
π electrons above and below the plane

blocks.head: NOTE ERROR
blocks.wrong: Notes say 'geometry: tetrahedral' for alkene shape
blocks.correct: Alkene carbons are sp² hybridized → TRIGONAL PLANAR geometry with 120° bond angle
blocks.reason: Tetrahedral (109.5°) applies to sp³ hybridized alkanes. Alkenes are sp² → trigonal planar.

blocks.head: Why π-bond Is Reactive
blocks.body: π-bond electrons are NOT along the internuclear axis. They are above and below the line. They act as nucleophile (attack at +ve).
items: π electrons are delocalized → easily available
Acts as nucleophile → makes alkenes highly reactive
π-bond is weaker than σ-bond → breaks more easily

blocks.label: Electrophile
blocks.text: Electrophile is a species that can act as electron pair acceptor. Represented by E⁺.

blocks.label: Nucleophile
blocks.text: Nucleophile is a species that can act as electron pair donor. Represented by Nu⁻.

blocks.label: Carbocation (Carbonium Ion)
blocks.text: Radical having C⁺ is called a carbocation or carbonium ion. C⁺ has empty orbital of p type. C⁺ is sp² hybridized.

blocks.head: Types of Carbocations
blocks.body: Classified by number of R groups (alkyl groups) bonded to C⁺:
items: Methyl (CH₃⁺): C⁺ has no R or C bonded to it
Primary (1°): C⁺ bonded with one R (directly bonded with one other carbon) → R–CH₂⁺
Secondary (2°): C⁺ bonded with two R-groups → R–CH⁺–R
Tertiary (3°): C⁺ bonded with three R-groups → R–C⁺(–R)–R

blocks.head: Stability Order
blocks.body: Stability of carbocations:
blocks.eq:
Tertiary > Secondary > Primary > CH₃⁺
Reactivity decreases with stability

blocks.label: Inductive Effect
blocks.text: Polarization (unequal distribution of electrons) caused by sigma bond. The polarization of a σ-bond due to electron withdrawing or electron donating effect of adjacent atoms is called inductive effect. Represented by I.

blocks.head: Inductive Effect — Types
blocks.body: Two types of inductive effect:
items: Positive (+I): electron donating effect. Groups: NH₂, OH, alkyl groups (–CH₃, –C₂H₅)
Negative (–I): electron withdrawing effect. Groups: –C=O (OH), –C≡N

blocks.head: Stability and +I Effect
blocks.body: Stability of C⁺ increases with more +I groups. More alkyl groups → more electron donation → C⁺ becomes less positive → more stable.
items: 3° carbocation: 3 alkyl groups donate electrons → MOST STABLE
1° carbocation: 1 alkyl group → LEAST STABLE
Inductive effect plays important role in stability of carbocation because of hyperconjugation

blocks.head: Polarization of Non-Polar Bond
blocks.body: Polarization of a non-polar bond due to presence of neighbouring polar bond is called inductive effect. Bond is induced (neighbour's polar bond induces the effect).

blocks.head: –I Effect (Negative Inductive)
blocks.body: Groups like halogens withdraw electrons → negative inductive effect. Causes permanent dipole. Halogen atom holds negative charge; carbon becomes partial positive.
blocks.eq:
C₄–C₃–C₂–C₁–Cl
(δ⁺⁺)(δ⁺⁺)(δ⁺)(δ⁻)
Effect decreases down the chain

blocks.head: Types of Reactions
blocks.body: Alkenes mainly undergo electrophilic addition reactions. Other reactions include oxidation, combustion, polymerization.

blocks.label: Electrophilic Addition Reaction
blocks.text: The reactions in which an electrophile is added to the double bond of an alkene is called electrophilic addition reaction.

blocks.caption: Generalized mechanism of electrophilic addition to alkene: electrophile attacks C=C forming carbocation, then nucleophile attacks
blocks.alt: Two-step mechanism diagram with carbocation intermediate

blocks.label: Halogenation of Alkenes
blocks.text: Addition of halogen to a alkene is called halogenation.

blocks.head: Rate of Reaction (Halogenation)
blocks.body: Rate of halogenation of alkenes depends on:
items: EN of halogen
Size (inversely)
EN order: F₂ > Cl₂ > Br₂ > I₂
Size order: F₂ < Cl₂ < Br₂ < I₂
Reactivity order: F₂ > Cl₂ > Br₂ > I₂

blocks.head: Significance of Br₂/CCl₄ Test
blocks.body: Br₂/CCl₄ is reddish brown. Helps to distinguish between alkene and alkane:
items: Alkene + Br₂ (CCl₄) → colour discharged (decolorized)
Alkane + Br₂ (CCl₄) → no colour change

blocks.head: Mechanism of Halogenation
blocks.body: 3-step mechanism:
items: i) Formation of carbocation: X₂ molecules are non-polar (symmetrical). C=C is electron rich area. π-electrons are delocalized. π-electron causes polarization in halogen molecule → makes it unsymmetrical. CH₂=CH₂ + Br⁺–Br⁻ → CH₂⁺–CH₂Br
ii) Attack of nucleophile: X⁻ attacks at stable carbocation to form alkyl halide → CH₂⁺–CH₂Br + Br⁻ → CH₂Br–CH₂Br

blocks.label: Hydrohalogenation
blocks.text: Addition of hydrogen and halogen in alkene gives monohaloalkanes (alkyl halides) — called hydrohalogenation.

blocks.head: Alkenes May Be
blocks.body: Types of alkenes for addition:
items: Symmetrical: both carbons of double bond have equal substituents → does NOT follow Markovnikov's rule → one product
Unsymmetrical: carbons of double bond have unequal substituents → follows Markovnikov's rule → two products (major + minor)

blocks.label: Markovnikov's Rule
blocks.text: When a polar (unsymmetrical) reagent is added to an alkene, its positive part goes to the carbon with greater number of hydrogen atoms and negative part goes to carbon with less hydrogen atoms.

blocks.head: Mechanism of Hydrohalogenation
blocks.body: a) Formation of carbocation: electrons of π-bond are free to act as nucleophile. Attack positive end of nearby molecule to form carbocation.
items: R–CH=CH₂ + H⁺–X⁻ → R–CH⁺–CH₃ (2° carbocation) OR R–CH₂–CH₂⁺ (1° carbocation)
2° carbocation is more stable than 1° → so it is more favourable
b) Attack of Nu⁻: X⁻ attacks at stable carbocation to form alkyl halide

blocks.caption: Mechanism of HBr addition to propene showing 2° vs 1° carbocation and major/minor products

blocks.label: Hydrogenation
blocks.text: Hydrogenation means addition of molecular hydrogen to alkene.

blocks.head: Hydrogenation — Details
blocks.body: Conditions and products:
items: Conditions: Catalyst (Ni/Pt), Temperature 250–300°C
Product: Alkane

blocks.head: Significance of Hydrogenation
blocks.body: On industrial scale, this reaction converts vegetable oil to margarine (banaspati ghee).

blocks.label: Hydration
blocks.text: Addition of water is called hydration.

blocks.head: Hydration — Details
blocks.body: Details of hydration:
items: Hydrating agent: dil. H₂SO₄
Product: monohydroxy alcohol
If alkane is unsymmetrical → follows Markovnikov's rule

blocks.label: Halohydration
blocks.text: A reaction where alkenes react with halogens in the presence of water.

blocks.head: Halohydration
blocks.body: Product is halohydrin.
blocks.eq:
H₂C=CH₂ + Br₂ + H₂O → H₂C–CH₂ + HBr
                              |    |
                              Br  OH
                         (bromoethanol)

blocks.head: Termination step of Halogenation
blocks.body: In termination step of halogenation, two free radicals react together to form product. Free radical substitution of ethane results in formation of hexachloroethane.

blocks.label: Epoxidation
blocks.text: The epoxidation of alkenes gives an oxygen-containing three-membered cyclic ether called epoxide.

blocks.head: Epoxidation — Details
blocks.body: Details:
items: Reactant: limited supply of O₂ and alkene
Oxidizing agent: transition metal Ag (in form of Ag₂O)
Product: allylene epoxide or oxirane
Advantage: hydrolysis of epoxide gives trans-viccinal diol

blocks.head: Removal of Acidic Behaviour (in Epoxidation)
blocks.body: H₂O₂ produced is removed:

blocks.caption: Epoxidation of alkene using Ag catalyst and hydrolysis to trans-viccinal diol
blocks.alt: Alkene to epoxide to diol reaction steps

blocks.label: Ozonolysis
blocks.text: Breakdown of double bond with O₃ is called ozonolysis.

blocks.head: Ozonolysis — Mechanism
blocks.body: 3-step mechanism:
items: Step 1 — Formation of molo-ozonide: C=C + O₃ → molo-ozonide (unstable)
Step 2 — Formation of ozonide: unstable molo-ozonide rearranges to stable ozonide
Step 3 — Hydrolysis of ozonoid: ozonide + H₂O → 2 carbonyl compounds + H₂O₂

blocks.head: Significance of Ozonolysis
blocks.body: Helps to locate the position of double bond.
items: Alkene + O₃ →(Zn/CH₃OH, H₂O)→ carbonyl compounds (symmetrical alkene) OR mixture (unsymmetrical)
Condition: Zn (neutralizing agent) to remove H₂O₂
blocks.eq:
R–C=C–R + O₃ →(Zn/H₂O)→ R–C=O + O=C–R
                                    aldehyde  aldehyde

blocks.caption: Ozonolysis mechanism: molo-ozonide formation, ozonide rearrangement, hydrolysis to carbonyl compounds

blocks.label: Polymerization
blocks.text: Conversion of smaller units (low molecular weight) into larger units of high molecular weight is called polymerization.

blocks.head: Key Concepts in Polymerization
blocks.body: Important terms:
items: Mers → units
Polymer is a long chain of repeating units
Process in which monomers combine to form larger units → polymers
Polymerization may involve: formation of by-products (condensation) OR no by-products (addition polymerization)
Monomers have minimum 2 carbons

blocks.head: Identification of Monomers
blocks.body: Monomer is the smallest repeating unit of polymer. Identify structure of polymer.
items: π-bond breaks then new C–C bond forms
In polyethene: [–CH₂–CH₂–] is repeating unit
In PVC: –CH₂–CH– (with Cl) is repeating unit

blocks.head: Conclusion
blocks.body: Thus repeating units are monomers.

blocks.head: Example: Polymerization of Ethene
blocks.body: Conditions:
items: Zeigler-Nattle catalyst (Pt or Al)
High pressure and temperature
0.1% of O₂

blocks.head: Significance of Hydrogenation of Alkene (industrial)
blocks.body: On industrial scale, alkene hydrogenation converts vegetable oil to margarine. Eicosane is a straight-chain alkane with 20 carbons (C₂₀H₄₂).

items.q: Write the equation for the ozonolysis of ethene.
items.ans: CH₂=CH₂ + O₃ → [ozonide] →(Zn/H₂O)→ 2 HCHO (methanal) C₂H₄ + O₃ → C₂H₄O₃ → 2CH₂O

items.q: Give the epoxidation reaction of 2-Butene.
items.ans: CH₃–CH=CH–CH₃ + ½O₂ →(Ag)→ CH₃–CH–CH–CH₃ \O/ (epoxide) → (H⁺/H₂O) → CH₃–CH(OH)–CH(OH)–CH₃ (trans-diol)

items.q: How ozonolysis can indicate the position of a double bond?
items.ans:
Ozonolysis breaks the double bond and produces two carbonyl compounds (aldehydes/ketones). By identifying the products and working backwards, you can locate where the C=C was.

Example: If ozonolysis of an unknown alkene gives CH₃CHO + HCHO, then the original alkene was CH₃CH=CH₂ (propene).

blocks.label: Diene
blocks.text: A molecule containing two double bonds (C=C) is called a diene.

blocks.label: Conjugated Diene
blocks.text: In a conjugated diene, the double bonds in the carbon chain are separated by a single bond.

blocks.head: Why Conjugated Dienes Are Special
blocks.body: Adjacent double bonds allow overlap of p-orbitals on 3 or more adjacent atoms. This leads to delocalization of electrons which stabilizes the molecule.
items: π-bond overlap extends over the entire system
Delocalization of π electrons makes molecule more stable
Example: But-1,3-diene: CH₂=CH–CH=CH₂
Example: 2-Methylbut-1,3-diene (isoprene): CH₂=C(CH₃)–CH=CH₂

blocks.caption: Delocalization of π electrons across conjugated C=C–C=C system
blocks.alt: Four carbon chain with alternating double-single-double bonds and electron delocalization shown

blocks.head: Applications
blocks.body: Conjugated dienes like 1,3-butadiene are used in production of synthetic rubber. Conjugated structure allows polymerization into rubber-like chains.

items.q: Draw the structure of simple conjugated dienes such as Penta-1,3-diene.
items.ans: CH₂=CH–CH=CH–CH₃ Penta-1,3-diene

items.q: Illustrate the delocalization of electrons in conjugated dienes.
items.ans: In conjugated dienes (C=C–C=C), the p-orbitals on all four carbons are parallel and overlap. This allows π electrons to spread (delocalize) across all four carbons rather than being confined to one double bond. This is shown by curved arrows in resonance structures.

blocks.label: Isomerism
blocks.text: Two or more compounds having the same molecular formula but different structural formulae and properties are said to be isomers and the phenomenon is called isomerism.

blocks.head: Types of Structural Isomerism
blocks.body: Structural isomerism can be exhibited in 5 ways:

items.title: Chain Isomerism
items.body: — Difference in nature of carbon chain. Example: pentane, 2-methylbutane, 2,2-dimethylpropane all have formula C₅H₁₂.

items.title: Position Isomerism
items.body: — Difference in position of same functional group on the chain. Example: 1-chloropropane and 2-chloropropane (both C₃H₇Cl). Also but-1-ene and but-2-ene.

items.title: Functional Group Isomerism
items.body: — Same molecular formula but different functional groups. Example: CH₃OCH₃ (methoxymethane) and CH₃CH₂OH (ethanol) — both C₂H₆O.

items.title: Metamerism
items.body: — Unequal distribution of carbon atoms on either side of functional group. Example: ethoxy ethane and methoxy propane.

items.title: Tautomerism
items.body: — Shifting of proton from one atom to another within same molecule. Common in amino acids (zwitterion formation).

blocks.label: Stereoisomers
blocks.text: Stereoisomers are such compounds which possess the same structural formula, but differ with respect to the positions of the identical groups in space.

blocks.head: Types of Stereoisomerism
blocks.body: Two types:
items: i. Geometrical (cis-trans) isomerism
ii. Optical isomerism

items.q: Draw the displayed formula and names of isomers of C₄H₈ that could be an example of positional isomerism.
items.ans:
But-1-ene: CH₃–CH₂–CH=CH₂

But-2-ene: CH₃–CH=CH–CH₃

Both have formula C₄H₈ — differ in position of double bond → positional isomers.

items.q: What type of isomers are ethoxy methane (CH₃OC₂H₅) and propanol (C₃H₇OH)?
items.ans: Functional group isomers. Both have formula C₃H₈O but different functional groups: ether (–O–) vs alcohol (–OH).

blocks.label: Organic Redox Reactions
blocks.text: Oxidation-Reduction reactions that involve organic compounds are called organic redox reactions.

blocks.head: Organic Oxidation
blocks.body: During organic oxidation: oxygen is added OR hydrogen is removed.
items: Combustion: 2C₂H₆ + 7O₂ → 4CO₂ + 6H₂O
Ozonolysis: alkene + O₃ → carbonyl compounds (oxidative cleavage)
Epoxidation: alkene + O₂ → epoxide → diol
Primary alcohol + K₂Cr₂O₇/H₂SO₄ → carboxylic acid (Class 12 syllabus)

blocks.head: Organic Reduction
blocks.body: During organic reduction: hydrogen is added OR oxygen is removed.
items: Hydrogenation of alkene: C=C + H₂ →(Pt)→ C–C (alkane)
Reducing agents used: LiAlH₄, NaBH₄, Sn + conc. HCl
Reduction of nitriles to amines, amides to amines, carboxylic acid to primary alcohol

mcqs.q: An alkene undergoes ozonolysis followed by reduction with zinc dust and water to yield propanone and methanal. The alkene is:
mcqs.exp: 2-Methyl-2-butene: (CH₃)₂C=CHCH₃. Ozonolysis gives propanone (CH₃COCH₃) from (CH₃)₂C= end and methanal (HCHO) from =CHCH₃... Wait — methanal comes from =CH₂ end. Actually 2-Methyl-2-butene gives propanone + acetaldehyde. 2-Methylpropene (CH₂=C(CH₃)₂) gives methanal + propanone. Correct answer is C (2-Methylpropene) — ans index 2.

mcqs.q: Which of the following reagents is typically used for the acid-catalyzed hydration of alkenes to form alcohols?
mcqs.exp: Dilute H₂SO₄ is the hydrating agent. It catalyzes addition of water (H₂O) across the C=C double bond to give alcohol.

mcqs.q: Halogenation of alkanes is an example of:
mcqs.exp: Halogenation of alkanes proceeds via free radical mechanism: initiation (homolytic fission of X₂), propagation (Cl• attacks C–H), termination (radicals combine).

mcqs.q: Which of the following reactions can an alkane undergo?
mcqs.exp: Alkanes undergo substitution (halogenation) via free radical mechanism. They do NOT undergo addition (no π-bond) or polymerization.

mcqs.q: What is the first step in the electrophilic addition reaction of alkenes?
opts: Attack by an electrophile on the double bond
mcqs.exp: First step: electrophile (E⁺) attacks the π electrons of C=C double bond → forms carbocation intermediate. Then nucleophile attacks the carbocation.

mcqs.q: The addition of unsymmetrical reagent to an unsymmetrical alkene is in accordance with:
mcqs.exp: Markovnikov's rule: positive part of polar reagent adds to C with more H atoms, negative part to C with fewer H atoms.

mcqs.q: The most stable carbonium ion among the following is:
mcqs.exp: (CH₃)₃C⁺ is tertiary carbocation — 3 alkyl groups donate electrons (+I effect) → most stable. Stability: 3° > 2° > 1° > CH₃⁺.
(CH₃)₂C=CH₂ is an unsymmetrical alkene (different groups on each C of double bond) → Markovnikov's rule applies. CH₃CH=CHCH₃ is symmetrical. CH₂=CH₂ is also symmetrical.

mcqs.q: What intermediate is formed during the electrophilic addition of HBr to an alkene?
mcqs.exp: Electrophilic addition of HBr: H⁺ (electrophile) attacks π electrons → forms carbocation intermediate → Br⁻ (nucleophile) attacks carbocation → product.

mcqs.q: The enhanced stability of conjugated dienes compared to isolated dienes is primarily attributed to:
opts: Inductive effects of the double bonds
Increased s-character of the hybridised orbitals
Delocalization of π electrons across the conjugated system
Steric hindrance between the double bonds
mcqs.exp: In conjugated dienes (C=C–C=C), p-orbitals overlap across all 4 carbons → delocalization of π electrons → extra stability.

mcqs.q: Which of the following carbocations would be the least stable?
mcqs.exp: CH₃⁺ is methyl carbocation — no alkyl groups to donate electrons. Least +I effect → least stable.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is the repeating unit in the polymer poly(ethene)?
mcqs.exp: Polyethene is made from ethene (CH₂=CH₂). The C=C breaks and monomers link → repeating unit is –CH₂–CH₂– (C=C becomes C–C).

mcqs.q: In free radical halogenation of methane, diffused light produces a mixture of products because:
opts: Propagation continues stepwise replacing one H at a time
mcqs.exp: Diffused light initiates the reaction moderately. Propagation steps replace H atoms one at a time: CH₄ → CH₃Cl → CH₂Cl₂ → CHCl₃ → CCl₄.

mcqs.q: Br₂/CCl₄ test is used to distinguish between alkane and alkene because:
opts: Alkene decolorizes Br₂ (reddish-brown) while alkane does not
mcqs.exp: Alkene has π electrons → reacts with Br₂ via electrophilic addition → Br₂ colour discharged. Alkane has no π bond → no reaction with Br₂/CCl₄ → colour remains.

opts: Helps locate position of double bond in alkene
mcqs.exp: Ozonolysis breaks C=C and gives carbonyl products. By identifying these products, the position of the double bond in the original alkene can be determined.

mcqs.q: The product of halohydration of ethene with Br₂ and H₂O is:
mcqs.exp: Halohydration: H₂C=CH₂ + Br₂ + H₂O → CH₃–CHBr–OH (1-bromoethanol) + HBr. Br adds to one carbon, OH to the other.

mcqs.q: Which hybridization state does the C⁺ (carbocation) have?
mcqs.exp: C⁺ (carbocation) has an empty p orbital and three bonds. This corresponds to sp² hybridization → trigonal planar geometry.

sqs.q: Define: i) Cycloalkanes  ii) Isomerism  iii) Conjugated dienes  iv) Inductive effect
sqs.a:
i) Cycloalkanes: Cyclic saturated hydrocarbons in which carbon atoms are arranged in a ring. They have only single bonds. General formula CₙH₂ₙ. Example: cyclopropane (C₃H₆).

ii) Isomerism: The phenomenon in which two or more compounds have the same molecular formula but different structural formulae and properties. The compounds are called isomers.

iii) Conjugated Dienes: Dienes (molecules with two C=C double bonds) in which the double bonds are separated by a single bond (alternating pattern). π electrons are delocalized over all 4 carbons. Example: CH₂=CH–CH=CH₂ (but-1,3-diene).

iv) Inductive Effect: Polarization (unequal distribution of electrons) caused by sigma bond due to electron withdrawing or donating effect of adjacent groups or atoms. Represented by I. +I = electron donating; –I = electron withdrawing.

sqs.q: Differentiate between: Aliphatic and Aromatic Hydrocarbons
sqs.a:
Aliphatic Hydrocarbons:

  • Not aromatic
  • May be open chain (acyclic) or cyclic
  • May be saturated or unsaturated
  • Examples: alkanes, alkenes, alkynes, cycloalkanes

Aromatic Hydrocarbons:

  • Special class of cyclic compounds
  • Based on benzene ring (C₆H₆)
  • High carbon to hydrogen ratio
  • Have characteristic odour (aroma from Greek)
  • Examples: benzene, toluene, phenol

sqs.q: Differentiate between: Homolytic and Heterolytic Fission
sqs.a:
PropertyHomolyticHeterolytic
Electron distributionEven — one electron to each atomUneven — both electrons to one atom
ProductsTwo free radicalsTwo oppositely charged ions
Arrow typeHalf-headed (fish-hook)Full curly arrow
Occurs inPresence of light (atomic reactions)Ionic reactions
ExampleCl–Cl → Cl• + Cl•HO–H → OH⁻ + H⁺

Electrophile:

  • Electron pair acceptor
  • Represented by E⁺
  • Attacks electron-rich areas
  • Examples: H⁺, Br⁺, carbocations

Nucleophile:

  • Electron pair donor
  • Represented by Nu⁻
  • Attacks electron-poor (positive) areas
  • Examples: Br⁻, OH⁻, π electrons of alkenes

sqs.q: Explain why alkanes do not undergo addition reactions.
sqs.a:
Reason: Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons — all four valencies of each carbon are already satisfied by single (σ) bonds. There are no π bonds present.

Addition reactions require a π bond (like in alkenes/alkynes) because:

  • π electrons are loosely held and available for attack
  • The π bond breaks to allow new bonds to form with incoming atoms

In alkanes, all electrons are in σ bonds which are tightly held between nuclei — not available for addition. Therefore alkanes cannot undergo addition reactions and instead undergo substitution reactions.

sqs.q: Compare the carbocation stability in propene and 2-Butene.
sqs.a:
Propene (CH₃–CH=CH₂): When HX adds, a secondary (2°) carbocation forms at C2 and primary (1°) at C1.

CH₃–CH⁺–CH₃ (2° — more stable) CH₃–CH₂–CH₂⁺ (1° — less stable)

2-Butene (CH₃–CH=CH–CH₃): Both carbons of double bond are equivalent and both form secondary carbocations.

CH₃–CH⁺–CH₂–CH₃ (2°) CH₃–CH₂–CH⁺–CH₃ (2°)

Conclusion: 2-Butene gives equal stability carbocations on both sides. Propene gives a more stable 2° and a less stable 1° carbocation — so Markovnikov's product predominates in propene.

sqs.q: When propene (C₃H₆) undergoes electrophilic addition with HBr, it forms 2-bromopropane as the major product. Explain why 2-bromopropane is favored over 1-bromopropane, using the concept of carbocation stability.
sqs.a:
Reaction:

CH₃–CH=CH₂ + HBr → CH₃–CHBr–CH₃ (major) + CH₃CH₂CH₂Br (minor)

Explanation:

Step 1: H⁺ adds to the double bond. Two possible carbocations form:

  • At C2: CH₃–CH⁺–CH₃ (secondary, 2°) — 2 alkyl groups donate electrons (+I) → more stable
  • At C1: CH₃–CH₂–CH₂⁺ (primary, 1°) — 1 alkyl group → less stable

Step 2: Br⁻ preferentially attacks the more stable 2° carbocation.

Conclusion: 2-bromopropane is the major product because the reaction proceeds through the more stable secondary carbocation (Markovnikov's rule).

sqs.q: Explain the mechanism of free radical halogenation of methane with Cl₂ giving all three steps.
sqs.a:
Halogenation of methane with Cl₂ follows free radical mechanism with 3 steps:

1. Initiation: Homolytic fission of Cl–Cl bond by diffused light:

Cl₂ →(hν)→ Cl• + Cl•

2. Propagation: Cl• attacks C–H bond; carbon radical then attacks Cl₂:

CH₄ + Cl• → CH₃• + HCl CH₃• + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + Cl•

This cycle repeats, producing CH₂Cl₂, CHCl₃, CCl₄ progressively.

3. Termination: Two radicals combine:

Cl• + Cl• → Cl₂ CH₃• + Cl• → CH₃Cl CH₃• + CH₃• → C₂H₆

sqs.q: Describe ozonolysis of alkenes with mechanism and significance.
sqs.a:
Definition: Breakdown of C=C double bond with ozone (O₃) is called ozonolysis.

Mechanism (3 steps):

Step 1 — Formation of molo-ozonide:

C=C + O₃ → molo-ozonide (unstable cyclic intermediate)

Step 2 — Rearrangement to ozonide:

molo-ozonide → ozonide (more stable)

Step 3 — Hydrolysis:

ozonide + H₂O →(Zn)→ 2 carbonyl compounds + H₂O₂ (Zn is neutralizing agent — removes H₂O₂)

Significance: Helps locate position of double bond in an unknown alkene. Products are identified to determine original alkene structure.

lqs.title: Q8(a) — Hydrocarbons
lqs.q: Describe the reactions of alkenes. Include halogenation, hydrohalogenation, hydrogenation and hydration with mechanisms and conditions.

parts.label: INTRODUCTION — Alkenes and Their Reactivity
points: Alkenes are unsaturated hydrocarbons with C=C double bond and general formula CₙH₂ₙ
π electrons are delocalized and easily available → alkenes act as nucleophiles
Alkenes mainly undergo electrophilic addition reactions
C=C is region of high electron density → susceptible to attack by electrophiles

parts.label: 1. HALOGENATION
points: Addition of halogen (Cl₂ or Br₂) to alkene in inert solvent (CCl₄)
Equation: CH₂=CH₂ + Br₂ → CH₂Br–CH₂Br (1,2-dibromoethane)
Mechanism: π electrons polarize Br₂ → Br⁺ attacks C=C → carbocation forms → Br⁻ attacks
Significance: Br₂/CCl₄ test — alkene decolorizes reddish-brown Br₂, alkane does not
Reactivity order: F₂ > Cl₂ > Br₂ > I₂

parts.label: 2. HYDROHALOGENATION (Markovnikov's Rule)
points: Addition of HX (HCl, HBr, HI) to alkene gives monohalogenoalkane
Symmetrical alkene: one product only (no Markovnikov needed)
Unsymmetrical alkene: two products possible — Markovnikov's rule determines major product
Markovnikov's rule: H⁺ adds to C with more H atoms; X⁻ adds to C with fewer H atoms
Reason: more stable carbocation (2° or 3°) forms at more substituted carbon
Example: CH₃CH=CH₂ + HBr → CH₃CHBr–CH₃ (major, 2-bromopropane)

parts.label: 3. HYDROGENATION
points: Addition of molecular hydrogen (H₂) to alkene
Conditions: Catalyst Ni or Pt, Temperature 250–300°C
Product: alkane (saturated compound)
Equation: CH₂=CH₂ + H₂ →(Ni, 250-300°C)→ CH₃–CH₃
Industrial significance: vegetable oil + H₂ →(Ni)→ margarine (banaspati ghee)

parts.label: 4. HYDRATION
points: Addition of water to alkene
Hydrating agent: dilute H₂SO₄
Product: monohydroxy alcohol
Equation: CH₂=CH₂ + H₂O →(dil.H₂SO₄)→ CH₃CH₂OH (ethanol)
If alkene is unsymmetrical → follows Markovnikov's rule

parts.label: 5. MECHANISM OF ELECTROPHILIC ADDITION
points: Step 1 (Formation of carbocation): electrophile attacks π electrons of C=C → carbocation intermediate forms
Step 2 (Attack of nucleophile): nucleophile attacks the carbocation → product forms
The more stable (higher order) carbocation is preferentially formed
Stability: 3° > 2° > 1° > CH₃⁺ (due to +I effect of alkyl groups)
Reactivity (as intermediates): CH₃⁺ > 1° > 2° > 3°

lqs.title: Q8(a) — Alternative: Nomenclature and Structure
lqs.q: Explain the nomenclature of alkanes and alkenes with examples. Also explain the shapes of alkanes and alkenes.

parts.label: NOMENCLATURE OF ALKANES
points: General formula: CₙH₂ₙ₊₂. Methane is simplest member.
Rule 1: Select longest continuous chain → parent name
Rule 2: Number from end nearest substituent → lowest locant
Rule 3: With multiple substituents → list alphabetically, each with position number
Rule 4: Identical substituents → use di, tri, tetra as prefix
Sequence: position + name of substituent + parent chain name as alkane

parts.label: NOMENCLATURE OF ALKENES
points: General formula: CₙH₂ₙ. Suffix changes from –ane to –ene.
Rule 1: Parent chain must contain both carbons of C=C
Rule 2: Number chain from end nearest double bond
Rule 3: If double bond equidistant, number to give substituent lowest position
Sequence: position of substituent + name of substituent + position of double bond + parent chain as alkene
Example: 2-methyl-3-hexene, 2,5-trimethyl-3-hexene

parts.label: SHAPE OF ALKANES (sp³ hybridization)
points: Each C in alkane is sp³ hybridized — 4 equivalent hybrid orbitals
Tetrahedral shape with bond angle 109.5°
C–C bond length: 1.54 Å
All bonds are σ bonds: C–C (sp³–sp³ overlap), C–H (s–sp³ overlap)
No unhybridized orbital → no π bond → fully saturated

parts.label: SHAPE OF ALKENES (sp² hybridization)
points: Each C in alkene is sp² hybridized — 3 hybrid + 1 unhybrid pz orbital
Trigonal planar shape with bond angle 120°
C–C σ bond: sp²–sp² head-on overlap; C–H σ bonds: s–sp² overlap
C=C π bond: lateral overlap of parallel pz orbitals above and below plane
π electrons are delocalized → makes alkenes highly reactive toward electrophiles

quiz.q: What is the general formula of alkanes?
quiz.exp: Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons: CₙH₂ₙ₊₂. Example: methane CH₄ (n=1 → 2×1+2=4).

quiz.q: Which hybridization do carbons in alkenes have?
quiz.exp: Alkene carbons are sp² hybridized → trigonal planar with 120° bond angle and one unhybrid pz orbital forming the π bond.

quiz.q: Which type of bond is formed by lateral overlap of p-orbitals?
quiz.exp: π-bond is formed by lateral (sideways) overlap of parallel p-orbitals. σ-bond is formed by head-on overlap.

quiz.q: What is the product when alkene reacts with Br₂/CCl₄?
quiz.exp: Alkene + Br₂/CCl₄ → vicinal dihalide (e.g. CH₂=CH₂ + Br₂ → CH₂Br–CH₂Br). This is halogenation.

quiz.q: Alkanes are called paraffins because:
opts: They have little affinity for reagents
quiz.exp: Paraffins: Latin 'parum' = little, 'affins' = affinity. Alkanes have little affinity for polar reagents due to non-polar C–H and C–C bonds.

quiz.q: In the termination step of free radical halogenation, two CH₃• radicals form:
quiz.exp: CH₃• + CH₃• → C₂H₆. This is a minor termination product and evidence of free radical mechanism.

quiz.q: The C–C bond length in alkanes is:
quiz.exp: C–C single bond (σ bond) in alkanes has bond length 1.54 Å.

quiz.q: Markovnikov's rule applies to:
quiz.exp: Markovnikov's rule applies to addition of polar (unsymmetrical) reagents to unsymmetrical alkenes where two different products are possible.

quiz.q: In dehydration of alcohol to form alkene, the dehydrating agent is:
quiz.exp: Dehydration uses concentrated H₂SO₄ at 180°C. It removes H and OH from adjacent carbons to form C=C.

quiz.q: The stability order of carbocations is:
quiz.exp: Stability: 3° > 2° > 1° > CH₃⁺. More alkyl groups donate electrons (+I effect) → carbocation is more stable.

quiz.q: What does the Br₂/CCl₄ test show?
quiz.exp: Alkene decolorizes reddish-brown Br₂/CCl₄ → shows presence of C=C double bond (unsaturation). Alkane does not react.

quiz.q: Cycloalkanes have which general formula?
quiz.exp: Cycloalkanes: CₙH₂ₙ (same as alkenes but saturated cyclic). Example: cyclopropane C₃H₆.

quiz.q: Which step in free radical halogenation generates more radicals?
quiz.exp: Propagation step continues the chain: Cl• abstracts H → CH₃• forms → CH₃• attacks Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + new Cl•. Radicals are continuously regenerated.

quiz.q: The product of hydrogenation of ethene is:
quiz.exp: CH₂=CH₂ + H₂ →(Ni, 250-300°C)→ CH₃–CH₃ (ethane). Hydrogenation converts alkene to alkane.

quiz.q: In ozonolysis, the neutralizing agent Zn is used to:
quiz.exp: H₂O₂ is acidic and a by-product of ozonide hydrolysis. Zn removes it: H₂O₂ + Zn → ZnO + H₂O.

quiz.q: Repeating unit in polyethene is:
quiz.exp: Polyethene monomer is ethene (CH₂=CH₂). When polymerized, C=C becomes C–C → repeating unit is –CH₂–CH₂–.

quiz.q: Which carbocations are formed in electrophilic addition of HBr to propene?
quiz.exp: Propene (CH₃CH=CH₂) + H⁺: H adds to CH₂ end → CH₃–CH⁺–CH₃ (2°) or H adds to CH end → CH₃–CH₂–CH₂⁺ (1°). 2° is more stable → major product is 2-bromopropane.

quiz.q: What type of reaction is dehydrohalogenation of alkyl halide?
quiz.exp: Dehydrohalogenation removes H and X (halogen) from adjacent carbons → creates C=C double bond. This is an elimination reaction.

quiz.q: In conjugated dienes, double bonds are separated by:
quiz.exp: Conjugated diene pattern: C=C–C=C — two double bonds separated by one single bond. This allows π orbital overlap and electron delocalization.

quiz.q: Functional group isomers of C₂H₆O are:
quiz.exp: C₂H₆O has two functional group isomers: CH₃OCH₃ (dimethyl ether) and CH₃CH₂OH (ethanol). Different functional groups, same molecular formula.
